name: Cold compress / chilled washcloth

lead: A cold compress is a chilled washcloth or gel pack held against closed eyes, most often right after waking. People use it to take down morning puffiness and get a smoother, more rested-looking eye area within minutes.

Cold narrows blood vessels and compression limits fluid leaking into tissue, so less fluid sits under the eyes. Cold therapy is studied for swelling after injuries and some surgeries, including facial surgery, with mixed results; its effect on cosmetic under-eye puffiness specifically has not been tested in a trial.

paras: Users hold a damp cloth that has been chilled in the fridge, or a gel pack wrapped in cloth, over closed eyes for a few minutes, usually as part of a morning routine. It is often paired with sleeping elevated or cutting salt the night before. Effects are described as quick and temporary.

Ice or very cold packs placed directly on skin can cause cold burns, and cooling devices used without limits have been linked to frostbite and tissue damage. A cloth barrier is the usual precaution. Skin around the eyes is thin, so people with circulation disorders or cold sensitivity are advised to avoid it.

angle.text: A chilled cloth or gel pack on closed eyes narrows blood vessels and limits fluid, so the under-eye area looks flatter and more rested after waking. Cold therapy has been studied for injury and post-surgical swelling, while use on eye bags is based on user reports.

lead: A cold compress or chilled washcloth is a home practice of holding a cold, damp cloth, gel pack or chilled spoons against the closed eyes, typically after waking, to make the eye area look less puffy. The goal is a flatter lower lid and fresher, more awake-looking eyes within minutes, for example before work, photos or events.

Periorbital puffiness is swelling around the eyes caused almost always by fluid build-up, and is often worst on waking because fluid shifts while lying flat.[1] Wikipedia lists applying a cold compress near the eye for short-term relief among its suggested measures, explaining that cold narrows blood vessels and reduces fluid leakage.[1] Cold lowers tissue temperature and constricts vessels, while compression limits fluid leakage.[2]

Cold therapy generally is used for pain and swelling after soft-tissue injury and some surgeries, including facial surgery, where a systematic review found it decreased pain and swelling on days two or three.[2] Evidence for cryotherapy is mixed in other settings; one systematic review found insufficient evidence in ankle sprains.[2] Randomized trials have also examined cold compresses in third-molar surgery recovery and in treatments for allergic conjunctivitis and induced bruising, but no trial of cold compresses for cosmetic under-eye puffiness has been published.[3][4][5]
infobox: Chilled cloth, gel pack, chilled spoons

paras: Puffy lids and under-eye bags are caused mainly by fluid, and Wikipedia lists contributing factors including lying flat, ageing, allergies, crying, sleep loss, high dietary sodium and alcohol.[1] Cold compresses are a short-term measure suggested alongside head elevation during sleep and lifestyle changes.[1]

Because the effect is on fluid rather than the underlying fat pad that enlarges with age, the visible change from a compress is described as temporary.[1] Severe or persistent puffiness may signal other medical conditions, and the article advises seeking care in that case.[1]

Cold slows metabolism and constricts blood vessels; after roughly ten minutes of intense cold a hunting reaction of alternating vasoconstriction and vasodilation is described.[2] Whether brief eye-area use produces visible changes has not been formally studied.
Direct ice on skin can cause a cryoburn, and wraps with a protective layer are described as safer.[2] Continuous cooling machines have led to reported frostbite and, in severe cases, tissue loss.[2]

No studies found on cold compresses for under-eye puffiness. Related research includes a systematic review reporting that cold compression after facial surgery reduces pain and swelling on days two or three,[2] a randomized trial comparing dexamethasone, ketoprofen and cold compress after impacted lower third molar surgery,[3] a randomized trial of nonpharmacologic treatments for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis,[4] and a randomized comparison of bruise-reduction treatments after laser-induced bruising.[5]
